nodes.date_label: 1944: Philosophical Fragments (limited circulation, with Max Horkheimer) · 1947: Dialectic of Enlightenment (revised publication, with Max Horkheimer) · 1950: The Authoritarian Personality (with Else Frenkel-Brunswik, Daniel J. nodes.description: A philosopher, social theorist and critic of music and mass culture associated with the Frankfurt School. edges.relationship: Treats exchange and the circulation of things as constitutive of value, with a political dimension.
edges.evidence_note: Own publisher-hosted introduction opening read; its explicit Simmel resource is retained, without inferring the rest of the chapter or a universal account of all commodities.

edges.relationship: Examines migration through both the transformation and retention of identities in dynamic communication.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2009 interview selected answer read; a specific theoretical resource for identity histories, not proof of direct influence on every historian using identity.

edges.relationship: Uses transnational and intercultural Black Atlantic formations to question national containers for cultural history.
edges.evidence_note: Own preface ix–xi read; the framework is explicitly provisional and does not claim complete coverage of Black intellectual history.

edges.relationship: Criticizes racial purity and closed identity categories while retaining the historical stakes of Black political culture and double consciousness.
edges.evidence_note: Own preface ix–xi read, including anti-anti-essentialism; this is not a claim that race has no material consequences or that all identity historians follow Gilroy.

edges.relationship: Defines social facts through externality and constraining force, rather than mere prevalence among individuals.
edges.evidence_note: Own chapter I opening read, including obligations, conventions and currents. His examples are attributed illustrations, not independently tested universal laws.

edges.relationship: Separates the causal explanation of institutions from their utility or present functions.
edges.evidence_note: Own chapter V section I opening read; changed uses and institutional survivals challenge explanation by usefulness alone. This is a methodological resource, without claiming every comparative historian accepted it.

edges.relationship: Makes individual psychology relational by including others as models, helpers, opponents and objects.
edges.evidence_note: Own Group Psychology chapter I read in full. Freud questions a sharp individual/group divide and an irreducible primitive group instinct; the explanation is attributed theory, not validated clinical evidence.

edges.relationship: Peter Gay treats psychoanalysis as an auxiliary resource for history while requiring evidence about the external social world.
edges.evidence_note: Named substantive reader Gay’s own interview answer read. This qualified reception claim does not equate psychoanalysis with an exhaustive historical explanation or endorse every Freudian hypothesis.

edges.relationship: Distinguishes political capacity and institutionalization from regime form and economic modernization.
edges.evidence_note: Own Political Order opening p. 1 and preserved prior source review support the distinction. This does not endorse order-first political prescriptions or verify national comparisons and predictions.

edges.relationship: Criticizes the civilizational model for personifying Islam and the West and suppressing their internal diversity and exchanges.
edges.evidence_note: Said’s own 2001 essay opening read. Edge is Said’s specific criticism of Huntington, with explicit attribution; Huntington’s whole 1996 book and complete reception debate unread.

edges.relationship: Uses the state of exception as a paradigm for examining the relation of law, anomy and governmental power.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview pp. 609–612 read. The emergency-to-normal-government thesis is attributed to Agamben; this is a philosophical paradigm rather than independent verification of an encompassing history of states.

edges.relationship: Agamben explicitly invokes Foucault’s panopticon and archaeology as resources for his paradigmatic method.
edges.evidence_note: Own interview pp. 610 and 613 read. Acknowledged methodological resource, not an assertion that Foucault endorsed Agamben or that their projects coincide.

edges.relationship: With Horkheimer, connects standardized cultural production to economic power rather than autonomous technological necessity.
edges.evidence_note: Joint primary chapter opening read. Authorship is collective; this does not attribute the whole chapter solely to Adorno or adopt its sweeping cultural judgments as findings.

edges.relationship: With Horkheimer, analyzes amusement’s continuity with work and the historical split between light and serious art.
edges.evidence_note: Joint primary chapter selected later paragraphs read. A conceptual resource for analyzing mass culture, not proof of direct transmission to all British cultural studies or a claim that popular art has no value.
